circuits.title: AND Gate
circuits.summary: The AND gate produces 1 only when every input is 1. With two inputs there is exactly one true row in its truth table.
objectives: Relate the AND symbol to the Boolean product Y = A · B.
Predict the output for all four input pairs before switching.
Recognise that a single 0 input forces the output to 0.
operation: Each input is a logic level. The output is the logical product of A and B, so it is high only when both switches are high. Any low input blocks the output.
In gate-level Verilog this behaviour is `and (y, a, b)`; in dataflow it is `assign y = a & b;`. The interactive diagram evaluates the same equation in JavaScript.
applications: Enabling a signal only when a device is selected and its data is valid.
Building the carry term of an adder and the enable path of a register.
observations: AND is not the same as OR: three of the four rows produce 0.
The output is 0 for 0·1, 1·0 and 0·0. Only 1·1 produces 1.
mistakes: Reading the symbol as OR because both inputs enter the flat side.
Assuming an unconnected input is high; an undriven input is unknown, not 1.
revision: AND is high only when all inputs are high.
The Boolean operator is multiplication: Y = A · B.
A single 0 is a blocking input for an AND gate.

table.caption: AND gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

outputs.name: Y
outputs.label: Y
outputs.help: High only when both inputs are high.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs: logic 1 means the switch is on and the node is high. Y is the active-high output. A dot in the Boolean equation means logical AND, not arithmetic multiplication.

circuits.title: OR Gate
circuits.summary: The OR gate produces 1 when at least one input is 1. It produces 0 only for the all-zero input row.
objectives: Relate the OR symbol to the Boolean sum Y = A + B.
Identify the single row that produces 0.
Distinguish logical OR from arithmetic addition.
operation: The output is the logical sum of A and B. If either switch is high the output is high; only 0 and 0 leave it low.
Verilog writes this as `assign y = a | b;`. The plus sign in Boolean algebra means OR, not binary addition, so 1 + 1 still produces 1.
applications: Combining multiple interrupt requests into one alert signal.
Detecting that any one of several fault conditions is active.
observations: Three of the four rows produce 1, the mirror image of AND.
Boolean 1 + 1 = 1; arithmetic 1 + 1 = 10 is a different operation.
mistakes: Expecting OR to carry like a binary adder.
Confusing the curved input side of OR with the flat input side of AND.
revision: OR is low only when every input is low.
The Boolean operator is addition: Y = A + B.
Logical addition never produces a carry.

table.caption: OR gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

outputs.name: Y
outputs.label: Y
outputs.help: High when at least one input is high.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs. Y is high when either input is high, and low only for A = 0 and B = 0. The plus sign in the equation means logical OR, so 1 + 1 still gives 1, with no carry.

circuits.title: NOT Gate (Inverter)
circuits.summary: The inverter produces the complement of its single input. It is the only one-input gate in the set.
objectives: Relate the triangle-and-bubble symbol to logical inversion.
Explain why the inverter has no two-input truth table.
Use inversion to form active-low signals.
operation: The output is the opposite of the input. A 0 becomes 1 and a 1 becomes 0, with no other possible result for a defined input.
Verilog writes the complement as `~a`. In gate-level form the primitive is `not (y, a)`. Inversion is the basis of NAND, NOR, XNOR and active-low control.
applications: Generating the select complement inside a 2:1 multiplexer.
Converting an active-high request into an active-low enable.
observations: The bubble at the output means inversion, not a separate gate.
An inverter cannot create a defined output from an unknown input; the result is unknown.
mistakes: Drawing the bubble on the input side and calling it an inverter.
Forgetting that two inverters in series restore the original polarity.
revision: NOT has one input and one output.
Y = ~A; the output is always the complement.
Two inversions cancel.

table.caption: NOT gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

circuits.io: A is the single active-high input and Y is its complement. When A is high, Y is low; when A is low, Y is high. The small circle at the gate output is the inversion bubble.

circuits.title: NAND Gate
circuits.summary: NAND is an AND gate followed by an inverter. It is low only when both inputs are high.
objectives: Read NAND as inverted AND.
Identify the only input pair that produces 0.
Explain why NAND is called a universal gate.
operation: The gate forms A · B and then complements the result. The output is 0 only for A = 1 and B = 1; every other row is 1.
Verilog dataflow uses `assign y = ~(a & b);` or the primitive `nand (y, a, b)`. NAND can implement NOT, AND, OR and any other combinational function when gates are combined.
applications: Building flash memory and SR latch structures from cross-coupled NAND gates.
Implementing arbitrary logic in a NAND-only ASIC library.
observations: NAND is the complement of AND, so every row is reversed.
The output is 1 for three of the four input pairs.
mistakes: Placing the bubble on the inputs instead of the output; that describes an OR gate with inverted inputs.
Forgetting the inversion when converting an AND design to NAND.
revision: NAND = NOT(AND).
Output 0 only for 1,1.
NAND is a universal gate.

table.caption: NAND gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

outputs.name: Y
outputs.label: Y
outputs.help: Low only when both inputs are high.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs and Y is the active-high output. NAND is an AND gate with an output bubble, so the output is the complement of A · B. The bubble marks the inversion, not an active-low input.

circuits.title: NOR Gate
circuits.summary: NOR is an OR gate followed by an inverter. It is high only when both inputs are low.
objectives: Read NOR as inverted OR.
Identify the only input pair that produces 1.
Use NOR as an active-low any-input detector.
operation: The gate forms A + B and then complements the result. The output is 1 only when A = 0 and B = 0.
Verilog dataflow uses `assign y = ~(a | b);` or the primitive `nor (y, a, b)`. Like NAND, NOR is universal and can build any combinational function.
applications: Detecting the all-clear condition in an active-low fault system.
Building cross-coupled NOR SR latches.
observations: NOR is the complement of OR, so exactly one row produces 1.
It is not an OR gate with inverted inputs; that different circuit is an AND gate.
mistakes: Mixing up NOR and NAND truth tables.
Assuming a NOR output is high when one input is low; both must be low.
revision: NOR = NOT(OR).
Output 1 only for 0,0.
NOR is a universal gate.

table.caption: NOR gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

outputs.name: Y
outputs.label: Y
outputs.help: High only when both inputs are low.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs and Y is the active-high output. NOR is an OR gate with an output bubble, so Y is the complement of A + B. It is not an OR gate with inverted inputs.

circuits.title: XOR Gate
circuits.summary: XOR produces 1 when the inputs differ. It is the parity detector and the sum term of a half adder.
objectives: Relate the XOR symbol to inequality detection.
Predict the output for equal and unequal inputs.
Connect XOR to the sum output of an adder.
operation: The output is high when exactly one input is high. Equal inputs produce 0, whether both are 0 or both are 1.
Verilog writes this as `assign y = a ^ b;`. XOR is associative, so a chain of XOR gates computes the parity of all its inputs.
applications: Parity generation and error detection.
The sum bit of half and full adders.
observations: XOR is not OR: 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 while 1 + 1 = 1.
The output detects difference, not the presence of a 1.
mistakes: Using OR when the equation calls for XOR.
Forgetting that an XOR chain inverts when an odd number of inputs is high.
revision: XOR = 1 when inputs differ.
Y = A ⊕ B.
XOR is the sum term of a half adder.

table.caption: XOR gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs. Y is high when exactly one input is high and low when the inputs match. The encircled plus sign is the XOR operator.

circuits.title: XNOR Gate
circuits.summary: XNOR is inverted XOR. It produces 1 when the inputs are equal, making it an equality detector.
objectives: Read XNOR as equality detection.
Relate XNOR to the complement of XOR.
Recognise the XNOR symbol and its output bubble.
operation: The output is high when A and B are both 0 or both 1. It is low when the inputs differ.
Verilog writes this as `assign y = ~(a ^ b);`. Cascaded XNOR gates are less common than XOR for parity because the inversion polarity depends on the number of stages.
applications: Comparing two single-bit signals for equality.
Detecting when a pair of bits matches in a larger comparator.
observations: XNOR is the exact complement of XOR.
It produces 1 for two rows, not one.
mistakes: Calling XNOR "not OR"; it is not NOR.
Forgetting the output bubble when drawing the symbol.
revision: XNOR = 1 when inputs are equal.
XNOR is the complement of XOR.

table.caption: XNOR gate truth table
table.note: Every row is checked by the interactive engine.

circuits.io: A and B are active-high inputs. Y is high when A and B match. The output bubble on the XOR symbol produces the complement, so XNOR is an equality detector.

circuits.title: Half Adder
circuits.summary: A half adder adds two one-bit inputs and produces a sum and a carry. It cannot accept a carry from a lower stage.
objectives: Derive sum and carry from the binary addition of two bits.
Explain why XOR gives the sum and AND gives the carry.
State why a half adder is insufficient for multi-bit addition.
operation: The sum output is A ⊕ B and the carry output is A · B. Adding 1 + 1 produces sum 0 and carry 1, which is binary 10.
The circuit is exactly one XOR gate and one AND gate sharing the same inputs. Verilog can describe it with two continuous assignments.
circuits.equation: S = A ⊕ B    C = A · B
applications: The least significant stage of a small adder where no incoming carry exists.
A teaching block for separating sum and carry behaviour.
observations: The arithmetic total is 2·C + S.
The half adder has no carry input, so it cannot be chained directly.
mistakes: Using OR for carry, which produces a carry for 0 + 1.
Trying to chain half adders without accounting for the missing carry input.
revision: S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B.
1 + 1 gives S = 0, C = 1.
A full adder is required for intermediate bit positions.

table.caption: Half adder truth table
table.note: The decimal column shows the arithmetic value A + B.

circuits.io: A and B are the two active-high addend bits. S is the active-high sum bit and C is the active-high carry bit. The arithmetic value is 2·C + S, so 1 + 1 produces S = 0 and C = 1.
circuits.verilog:
assign s = a ^ b;
assign c = a & b;

circuits.title: Full Adder
circuits.summary: A full adder adds three one-bit inputs: A, B and the carry-in from the previous stage. It is the reusable stage of a ripple-carry adder.
objectives: Compute sum and carry for all eight input combinations.
Use the propagate and generate terms to explain the carry.
Explain why a full adder can be chained.
operation: The sum is A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin. A carry is produced when A and B are both 1, or when exactly one of them is 1 and Cin is 1.
Using p = A ⊕ B and g = A · B, the carry is g + p·Cin. That form exposes why a carry can be generated locally or propagated from the previous bit.
circuits.equation: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin    Cout = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B)
applications: Each bit slice of a ripple-carry, carry-select or carry-lookahead adder.
Arithmetic inside an ALU and address-generation units.
observations: The full adder reduces to a half adder when Cin = 0.
With Cin = 1, the sum polarity of A ⊕ B is inverted and a carry can propagate.
mistakes: Leaving Cin out of the carry equation.
Using A + B for sum; sum is XOR, not OR.
revision: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin.
Cout = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B).
Four full adders make a four-bit ripple-carry adder.

table.caption: Full adder truth table
table.note: The decimal column shows A + B + Cin.

circuits.io: A, B and Cin are active-high one-bit inputs. S is the sum bit and Cout is the carry to the next stage. The arithmetic value is 2·Cout + S, covering totals from 0 to 3.
circuits.verilog:
assign s = a ^ b ^ cin;
assign cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b));

circuits.title: Half Subtractor
circuits.summary: A half subtractor computes A − B for two one-bit inputs, producing a difference and a borrow.
objectives: Derive the difference and borrow equations.
Explain why 0 − 1 needs a borrow.
Compare the half subtractor with the half adder.
operation: The difference is A ⊕ B. The borrow is ~A · B, because a borrow is needed only when A is 0 and B is 1.
The arithmetic result is difference minus 2·borrow. The half subtractor has no borrow input, so it cannot be chained without adding one.
applications: The least significant stage of a subtractor where no incoming borrow exists.
Teaching the relationship between subtraction and two's-complement addition.
observations: Difference uses XOR, the same as the half adder's sum.
Only 0 − 1 produces a borrow.
mistakes: Using A · ~B for borrow; that is the condition for no borrow.
Expecting a half subtractor to accept a borrow input.
revision: D = A ⊕ B, Bout = ~A · B.
0 − 1 gives D = 1, Bout = 1.
A full subtractor adds the borrow input.

table.caption: Half subtractor truth table
table.note: The result column shows A − B in decimal.

circuits.io: A is the active-high minuend bit and B is the active-high subtrahend bit. D is the difference and Bout is the borrow. Bout = 1 means the column needed to borrow 2 from the next stage.
circuits.verilog:
assign d = a ^ b;
assign bout = ~a & b;

circuits.title: Full Subtractor
circuits.summary: A full subtractor computes A − B − Bin, producing a difference and a borrow-out. It is the reusable stage of a multi-bit subtractor.
objectives: Compute difference and borrow for all eight combinations.
Explain how an incoming borrow changes the operation.
Relate the full subtractor to a full adder.
operation: The difference is A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin. A borrow-out occurs when A is less than B + Bin.
Equivalently, Bout = ~A·B + Bin·~(A ⊕ B). The second term propagates a borrow when the difference of A and B would be zero before the incoming borrow is applied.
circuits.equation: D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin    Bout = ~A·B + Bin·~(A ⊕ B)
applications: Each bit slice of a multi-bit subtractor.
Subtraction implemented as addition of a two's-complement value.
observations: With Bin = 0 the circuit behaves as a half subtractor.
A borrow can be generated locally or propagated from the previous stage.
mistakes: Using ~A·B alone and forgetting the propagated borrow term.
Mixing the borrow input with the carry input of a full adder.
revision: D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin.
Bout = ~A·B + Bin·~(A ⊕ B).
A full subtractor can be built by complementing the B input of a full adder.

table.caption: Full subtractor truth table
table.note: The result column shows A − B − Bin in decimal.

circuits.io: A, B and Bin are active-high one-bit inputs. D is the difference and Bout is the borrow out. The result represents A − B − Bin, which can be negative even though D itself is a single bit.
circuits.verilog:
assign d = a ^ b ^ bin;
assign bout = (~a & b) | (bin & ~(a ^ b));

circuits.title: 4-Bit Ripple-Carry Adder
circuits.summary: Four full adders chained by their carries add two four-bit numbers, with carry-out and signed overflow flags.
objectives: Trace a carry from bit 0 through bit 3.
Distinguish unsigned carry-out from signed overflow.
Predict the result for boundary cases such as 15 + 1 and 8 + 8.
operation: The least significant full adder receives Cin. Its carry-out feeds the next stage, and so on. The four sum bits form S = A + B + Cin modulo 16.

Carry-out is the bit beyond bit 3. Overflow is different: it is set when two operands with the same sign produce a result with the opposite sign. Compare 15 + 1, which sets carry but not overflow, with 8 + 8, which sets both.
circuits.equation: S = (A + B + Cin) mod 16    Cout = carry beyond bit 3    Overflow = (A3 == B3) · (S3 != A3)
applications: The arithmetic core of a small ALU or address incrementer.
A concrete example of carry propagation delay in a datapath.
observations: The 512-row exhaustive table is verified by the engine test; the table below shows the boundary cases.
Unsigned carry and signed overflow answer different questions and can be set independently.
mistakes: Using carry-out as the overflow flag.
Reversing the bit order so A3 feeds the least significant stage.
revision: Four full adders form a four-bit ripple-carry adder.
Cout is the carry beyond bit 3; overflow uses the sign bits.
15 + 1 gives S = 0, Cout = 1, Overflow = 0.
8 + 8 gives S = 0, Cout = 1, Overflow = 1.

table.caption: 4-bit ripple-carry adder truth table
table.note: All 512 combinations of A, B and Cin are listed. The decimal columns show the operands and the 4-bit sum; Cout and OVF are separate flags.

circuits.title: 4:1 Multiplexer
circuits.summary: A 4:1 multiplexer routes one of four data inputs to a single output, selected by a two-bit code.
objectives: Explain how the select code chooses a data input.
Write the multiplexer expression as a sum of gated terms.
Verify that only the selected data bit reaches the output.
operation: The two select bits decode to one of four channels. The selected channel's data value appears at Y; the other channels are ignored.
The Boolean form is Y = ~S1·~S0·D0 + ~S1·S0·D1 + S1·~S0·D2 + S1·S0·D3. Only one product term is active for a given select code.
applications: Selecting one of several sensors, registers or buses for a shared data path.
Building a barrel shifter from a tree of multiplexers.
observations: The select code chooses a channel; the data value itself does not affect which channel is chosen.
A 2:1 multiplexer needs one select line; a 4:1 needs two.
mistakes: Reversing S1 and S0, which swaps channels 1 and 2.
Confusing a multiplexer with a decoder; a decoder does not route data.
revision: A 4:1 mux has four data inputs, two select lines and one output.
Y equals the selected D input.
The select code is a binary channel number.

table.caption: 4:1 multiplexer truth table
table.note: All 64 combinations of S1, S0 and D3…D0 are listed. Y follows the selected data input.

circuits.io: D0…D3 are active-high data inputs. S1 and S0 form the active-high binary channel number, with S1 the high bit. Y follows the selected data input; the other data inputs have no effect on Y.

circuits.title: 1:4 Demultiplexer
circuits.summary: A 1:4 demultiplexer routes one data input to one of four outputs, selected by a two-bit code. All unselected outputs are 0.
objectives: Explain the difference between a demultiplexer and a decoder.
Show that every unselected output is driven to 0.
Trace the data input through the selected output.
operation: The select code chooses one output. That output follows Din, while the other three are forced to 0. When Din = 0, all four outputs are 0 regardless of the select code.
This is a decoder with the data input acting as an enable. The one-hot property comes from the select decode; the data input gates the selected line.
applications: Distributing one serial data stream to one of several destinations.
Routing a clock or enable to a selected register bank.
observations: Unlike a decoder, a demultiplexer can produce an all-zero output when Din is 0.
The unselected outputs are driven low, not left floating.
mistakes: Assigning only the selected output and leaving the others undriven.
Using OR instead of AND, which forces outputs high when Din is 0.
revision: A 1:4 demux has one data input, two select lines and four outputs.
Exactly one output follows Din; the others are 0.
Din = 0 produces all zeros.

table.caption: 1:4 demultiplexer truth table
table.note: Every input and select combination is listed.

inputs.name: Din
inputs.label: Din
inputs.help: Data input that is routed to one output.

circuits.io: Din is the active-high data input and S1/S0 form the channel number. Exactly one output follows Din; the other three outputs are driven low. When Din = 0 every output is low, whatever the select code.

circuits.title: 2-to-4 Decoder with Enable
circuits.summary: A 2-to-4 decoder asserts exactly one of four outputs for each input code. An enable input can force all outputs low.
objectives: Map a two-bit code to its one-hot output.
Explain the effect of the active-high enable.
Distinguish a decoder from a demultiplexer.
operation: When EN = 1, the input code selects one output and drives it high. The other outputs stay low. When EN = 0, all four outputs are forced low.
Each output is a product term: Y0 = EN·~A1·~A0, Y1 = EN·~A1·A0, and so on. The enable makes the decoder safe to place on a shared bus.
applications: Selecting one register, memory bank or peripheral from a shared bus.
Driving a seven-segment display through a code converter.
observations: A decoder does not pass a data value; it passes an enable to the selected output.
The enable prevents an unintended one-hot pattern during reset.
mistakes: Forgetting the enable term in each output equation.
Calling a decoder a demultiplexer when no data input is gated.
revision: A 2-to-4 decoder has two select bits and four one-hot outputs.
EN = 0 forces all outputs to 0.
Only one output is high when EN = 1.

table.caption: 2-to-4 decoder truth table
table.note: All enable and input combinations are listed.

inputs.name: EN
inputs.label: EN
inputs.help: Active-high enable. Low forces every output low.

circuits.io: EN is an active-high enable. A1 and A0 form the active-high address. When EN = 1 exactly one output is high and the rest are low; when EN = 0 all four outputs are forced low.

circuits.title: 4-to-2 Priority Encoder
circuits.summary: A priority encoder converts four request lines into a two-bit code, choosing the highest-numbered active request and reporting whether any request exists.
objectives: Explain priority when more than one request is active.
Read the valid output as an any-request flag.
Write the encoder outputs as Boolean expressions.
operation: R3 has the highest priority, then R2, R1 and R0. The code reports the highest active request. If no request is active, valid = 0 and the code is 00.
The outputs are code1 = R3 + R2 and code0 = R3 + ~R2·R1. The valid flag is the OR of all requests. The code bits are not simply the two highest request lines because priority changes the encoding.
circuits.equation: Valid = R3 + R2 + R1 + R0    Code1 = R3 + R2    Code0 = R3 + ~R2·R1
applications: Interrupt controllers that must identify the highest-priority request.
Arbitration in a shared bus or memory port.
observations: The output code can be 00 even when a request is active only if that request is R0; valid distinguishes this from the no-request case.
Multiple active inputs are allowed; the highest one wins.
mistakes: Ignoring priority and treating the input as one-hot only.
Forgetting the valid flag, which makes R0 and no-request indistinguishable.
revision: Priority order: R3, R2, R1, R0.
Valid is the OR of all requests.
The code identifies the highest active request.

inputs.name: R3
inputs.label: R3
inputs.help: Request 3. Higher numbers have higher priority.

inputs.name: R2
inputs.label: R2
inputs.help: Request 2. Higher numbers have higher priority.

inputs.name: R1
inputs.label: R1
inputs.help: Request 1. Higher numbers have higher priority.

inputs.name: R0
inputs.label: R0
inputs.help: Request 0. Higher numbers have higher priority.

outputs.name: Valid
outputs.label: Valid
outputs.help: High when any request is active.

circuits.io: R3…R0 are active-high request lines, with R3 highest priority. Code1 and Code0 report the highest active request. Valid is high when any request is active, which distinguishes request R0 from the no-request case.
circuits.verilog:
assign valid = |r;
assign code  = r[3] ? 2'd3 : r[2] ? 2'd2 : r[1] ? 2'd1 : 2'd0;

circuits.title: 4-Bit Magnitude Comparator
circuits.summary: A 4-bit comparator compares two unsigned binary numbers and asserts one of three outputs: greater than, equal or less than.
objectives: Compare two four-bit unsigned values and predict the active output.
Explain why only one of the three outputs is high.
Distinguish unsigned comparison from signed comparison.
operation: The comparator subtracts B from A internally and examines the result. In this demonstration the values are unsigned, so 1111 (15) is greater than 0000 (0).
Exactly one output is asserted: GT when A > B, EQ when A = B, and LT when A < B. Equal comparison can also be built as an XNOR of each bit pair ANDed together.
circuits.equation: GT = (A > B)    EQ = (A == B)    LT = (A < B)
applications: Address decoding, loop counters and conditional branch hardware.
Sorting and threshold detection in a datapath.
observations: The comparison here is unsigned. 1000 is 8, not −8.
GT, EQ and LT are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
mistakes: Using signed values without changing the comparison rule.
Assuming more than one output can be high at the same time.
revision: A 4-bit unsigned comparator has 256 input combinations.
GT, EQ and LT are one-hot.
EQ is true only when all four bit pairs match.

circuits.title: D Flip-Flop with Enable and Reset
circuits.summary: A positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop stores one bit. Enable decides whether a clock edge loads D, and an asynchronous reset clears Q immediately.
circuits.scope: D, EN, CLK, RST · Q and Q̄ · state
objectives: Distinguish a clock edge from a clock level.
Explain the roles of D, enable and asynchronous reset.
Predict Q after a sequence of load, hold and reset operations.
operation: Q changes only on a rising clock edge, and only when EN = 1. With EN = 0 the flip-flop holds its previous value even if D changes. Reset is asynchronous: asserting RST clears Q immediately, without waiting for a clock edge.

The next-state equation is Qnext = RST ? 0 : (rising edge ? (EN ? D : Q) : Q). This is sequential behaviour: the output depends on the stored state as well as the current inputs. The clock button below produces one rising edge.
applications: Registers, pipelines and state machines.
Debouncing and synchronising a mechanical input to a clock domain.
observations: Changing D while the clock is not rising must not change Q.
Reset is asynchronous in this model, so it acts even with no clock edge.
Q̄ is always the complement of Q while Q is defined.
mistakes: Treating a high clock level as a continuous load; only the edge loads.
Forgetting the enable and expecting every edge to capture D.
revision: A D flip-flop captures D on the active clock edge.
Enable gates the capture; reset clears the state.
State changes only on an edge, not on a level.

circuits.io: D is the active-high data input. EN is an active-high enable and RST is an active-high asynchronous reset. Q is the stored state and Q̄ is its complement. The clock is an explicit control: only a rising edge can update Q.
